column1: What is the primary physical constraint that cascades through all mobile OS architectural decisions?
column2: Thermal dissipation limits in a passively-cooled, battery-powered device (junction temps below 85°C, power budgets rarely exceeding 5W), which forces throttling, scheduler quanta, memory policies, and security domain granularity.

column1: How does the mobile security model invert traditional desktop ambient authority assumptions?
column2: Mobile apps start with zero authority by default—reading only their own sandbox container—and must explicitly request permission grants mediated by OS frameworks, rather than possessing ambient access restricted only by discretionary controls.

column1: What formal contract defines the declarative UI paradigm, and what capabilities does it enable?
column2: UI = f(state) — the UI is a deterministic function of application state. This determinism enables hot-reload, time-travel debugging, and UI snapshot testing (used by Flutter, React Native, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose).

column1: What is the retained-mode invariant in mobile UI rendering, and why does it matter?
column2: Mobile UI systems maintain a persistent scene graph/view hierarchy (unlike immediate-mode rendering like OpenGL where every draw call is reissued each frame). Code describes changes to the graph, not raw pixels, allowing the system to diff and reconcile minimal mutations instead of full redraws.

column1: Why is data in a mobile app's page cache considered volatile even after a write call like sqlite3_exec?
column2: Because the write has only reached the kernel's page cache, not the flash controller's write buffer or stable storage—it has not crossed the fsync boundary, so sudden power loss causes data loss.

column1: What are the four conceptually distinct state layers in mobile persistence, and why must they be treated differently?
column2: Ephemeral UI state, authentication credentials, in-progress drafts, and local replicas of server-side data—each has different durability, access pattern, and failure semantics; conflating them causes over-engineering or catastrophic data loss.

column1: What is the central invariant governing mobile concurrency architecture?
column2: The main (UI) thread must never block; any work exceeding ~16ms on it causes dropped frames and non-responsiveness, forcing all non-latency-sensitive work (network, DB, decoding, crypto, parsing) to background threads.

column1: Why can't mobile apps rely on simple TCP-level signals to distinguish network failure types?
column2: TCP/IP provides no native mechanism to distinguish slow, temporarily blocked, or permanently severed connections (e.g., a SYN timeout could mean packet loss, congestion, firewall issues, or real unavailability), requiring application-layer reachability detection and active probing.

column1: What is the fundamental invariant governing offline sync architecture in mobile apps?
column2: Every state mutation must be recorded as an immutable, totally-ordered event (event-sourcing/append-only log) that can be replayed, merged, or discarded via design-time conflict resolution policies, turning sync into log reconciliation rather than snapshot diffing.

column1: What invariant must hold for a cross-platform mobile architecture to remain viable across OS evolution?
column2: Interface stability under platform evolution: shared logic must bind to stable low-level C ABIs (e.g., libSystem.dylib, Bionic libc) that platform vendors maintain backwards compatibility for, rather than volatile high-level frameworks.

column1: Name the three canonical cross-platform mobile architecture approaches and their core mechanism.
column2: 1) Native module integration (C/C++ compiled to .so/.dylib via FFI), 2) JavaScript bridge architectures (React Native, async message queues to native code), 3) AOT compilation frameworks (Flutter, KMM—single codebase compiled to native binaries per platform).

column1: Why does f2fs's log-structured design matter for Android storage compared to ext4?
column2: f2fs (Flash-Friendly File System) minimizes write amplification against NAND flash via its log-structured design, which improves battery life and storage longevity on constrained mobile devices.
